ACT-SC6-P1-Q1.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous. I decoded the axis independently before looking at the key: Fig 1 has 0 min at y=132 and 50 min at y=22, i.e. 2.2 px/min. The Additive M marker at 5 mg/L is the open diamond spanning y=94.4-99.2, centre 96.8 -> (132-96.8)/2.2 = 16.0 min exactly. Unlabelled minor ticks at y=121/99/77/55/33 (= 5/15/25/35/45) are present on the left axis, so 16 is read as 'one tick above 15', not estimated in a bare 10-unit gap. At 5 mg/L the four markers sit at 30/21/16/9 min, separated by 11-13 px, and the marker shapes (filled circle, open square, open diamond, filled triangle) are all distinguishable at the 375 px phone render. No tick, marker or label was hard to resolve. Distractors are the other three curves' values at the same x - the canonical ACT wrong-curve set, all real. CROSS-ITEM: the option set is four bare values; nothing is recoverable without the figure.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q2.pick: Additive J gave its greatest clearing time of the concentrations tested
ACT-SC6-P1-Q2.note: FIGURE READ: resolvable, but this is the item with the thinnest margin in Fig 1 and it deserves naming. The concentration comes from the passage, not the figure (Exp 2 = 10 mg/L), so the figure work is checking four maxima. J: 12/30/44/36/21, peak at 10 - the drop from 44 to 36 is 17.6 px, unmissable. K: 12/21/27/29/30, still rising, peak at 20. L: 12/9/8/18/36, 10 mg/L is its MINIMUM. M: 12/16/40/42/41 - and here is the tight one: M at 10 mg/L (y=44.0) vs 15 mg/L (y=39.6) is a 2 min difference = 4.4 px, against a diamond 4.8 px tall. I checked this at the real render width (the app forces the SVG to w-full inside a max-w-md card, so ~340-416 px) and the 15 mg/L diamond does sit visibly higher, and the dash-dot segment between them visibly rises. So M is refuted. Even under the worst reading (M flat from 10 to 20) M would be a TIE at 10, never a clear peak, while J's peak is unambiguous - so no second option is defensible. Options are one identical frame with only the additive letter varying, which is the clean (non-leaky) option shape: every option satisfies the stem equally and only the figure discriminates. CROSS-ITEM: see Q6 note on the letter-spread tell.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q3.note: FIGURE READ: resolvable at the real render size, but this is the item I came closest to voting false on, and the author's 'easy' label is wrong. Fig 2 is 0 min at y=234, 50 at y=174 = 1.2 px/min, and it is labelled ONLY at 0/25/50 with no minor ticks, so nothing in Fig 2 can be read to better than about +/-2 min. The key comparison IS 2 min: K unstirred 27 (y=201.6) vs stirred 29 (y=199.2), a 2.4 viewBox-px gap, ~2.6 device px on a 375 px phone. The near-miss is L: 8 vs 7, a 1.2 px gap in the opposite direction, and the open (stirred) bars carry a 1 px stroke centred on the rect edge while the filled bars are unstroked, so every open bar renders 0.5 px (0.42 min) taller than its value - that eats 40 percent of L's already-tiny gap and makes the L pair read as a dead tie. I rendered at 375 px and inspected at 7x nearest-neighbour before deciding: K's open bar is plainly taller and clears the 25-min gridline that its filled partner sits on, whereas L reads as tied-or-slightly-lower. A tie is not 'GREATER', so L is not defensible and exclusivity holds. But the margin is thin by construction and the stroke artefact pushes in the wrong direction; I would widen the Fig 2 gridlines to every 10 min, or stroke the filled bars identically, or open K's gap to 4-5 min. Distractors: L (-1) is strong and M (-4) is fair, but J (44 -> 17) is a throwaway - nobody reads a two-and-a-half-fold collapse as an increase, so this is effectively a 3-option item. CROSS-ITEM: Q4's stem asserts that stirring LOWERED one additive far more than any other, which frames stirring as a lowering effect and, if anything, biases a student against finding the one increase here - mild coupling, in the harmless direction.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q4.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous in both figures. Fig 2 drops: J 44 -> 17 = -27 min (a 32.4 px collapse), K +2, L -1, M -4. 'Far more than any other' is not close - J is the only candidate and the selection step needs no fine reading at all. Then Fig 1, Additive J at 15 mg/L: filled circle at cy=52.8 -> (132-52.8)/2.2 = 36.0 min exactly, sitting between the 30 and 40 gridlines and right on the unlabelled 35 minor tick's neighbourhood; the nearest competing marker at that x is M's diamond at 42 min, 13.2 px away. No resolution difficulty. Distractors are the other three curves at 15 mg/L (M 42, K 29, L 18), each reachable by a named wrong selection rule - tallest bars, the one that rose, the shortest bars. Genuinely strong. DIFFICULTY: the author calls this hard; I would call it medium. Chained two-figure reads are standard ACT Science, and because J's drop is visually enormous the 'select the series' step costs nothing - the hard version of this item would have two additives with comparable drops.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q5.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous. Additive K (dashed, open squares) is 21 min at 5 mg/L (y=85.8) and 27 min at 10 mg/L (y=72.6), both exact on my decoded scale, and the segment between them is drawn as a straight polyline leg, so 7.5 mg/L interpolates to exactly 24.0 min - the midpoint. 24 is the only option lying strictly between the two bracketing plotted values, so no second option survives. The K squares are well separated from the other three series across that whole interval; nothing was hard to resolve. Distractors are well chosen individually: 21 (read the nearer plotted point instead of interpolating), 16 (M's value at the same x - wrong curve), 12 (the additive-free level at the left edge). CROSS-ITEM - THE ONE REAL LEAK I FOUND, and it is mild: Q5 reuses 16 and 21 from Q1's option set, and a student who has just solved Q1 already knows 16 = M at 5 mg/L and 21 = K at 5 mg/L. Taking the batch in order, they can eliminate both as 'values at 5, not 7.5' plus 12 as the plotted baseline, and reach 24 by elimination without performing the interpolation the item is testing. It still requires the figure, so it is not a blind leak - but Q5's independent difficulty is lower than labelled for anyone answering sequentially. Cheapest fix: interpolate on a different curve, or move the 7.5 mg/L point to a stretch whose endpoints are not already in Q1's options.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q6.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous, and the baseline is properly signposted. The additive-free mean is the single open circle at 0 mg/L, y=105.6 -> 12.0 min; the passage and the caption both identify it, and it is drawn larger (r=2.6, white fill, heavier stroke) than any data marker, so it is not mistakable for a series point. L is 9 min at 5 and 8 min at 10 - 6.6 and 8.8 px clear of the 12-min level, well outside any reading error. J's minimum is 21, K's is 21, M's is 16; all three sit at least 8.8 px above the baseline at every concentration, so none can be defended. Exclusivity is solid. ONE MARKER CAVEAT, the only one in the whole figure: the filled triangles (Additive L) are not vertically centred on their data point - apex 2.3 px above, base 1.7 px below - so the triangle's visual centroid reads about 0.17 min low. It is far below the resolution that matters for any of the six items, but it is the one marker whose centre I could not place by eye as confidently as the circles, squares and diamonds, and it is worth fixing if a future item ever needs a 1-min L read. FIGURE-AS-A-WHOLE, checking the author's 'reconstructs exactly' claim independently: it holds. Every one of the 24 Fig 1 values and 8 Fig 2 values lands on an exact integer minute under the decoded scales (2.2 and 1.2 px/min) with zero rounding drift; the four Fig 2 unstirred bars (44/27/8/40) match the four Fig 1 values at 10 mg/L exactly, which is a real internal cross-check and it passes; line style and marker shape match the caption for all four series; the right-edge J/K/L/M labels match the 20 mg/L endpoints. Two drawing defects beyond the triangle: the open Fig 2 bars' centred 1 px stroke inflates them 0.5 px relative to the unstroked filled bars (see Q3), and the Fig 2 legend block sits inside the plot area above Additive L's bars - harmless at these values but it would collide if L ever exceeded about 40 min. CROSS-ITEM GUESSABILITY, batch-wide: I checked this before grading individual items and the batch is close to the best case for ACT Science. Every option set is either four bare numeric values (Q1, Q4, Q5) or four bare additive names (Q3, Q6) or one identical sentence frame with only the letter varying (Q2) - by the axis-alignment test in CLAUDE.md, nothing here differs along the axis the stem names, so there is no options-only route into any item. Key positions are 2/4/1/4/3/1, i.e. A x2 B x1 C x1 D x2, no slot dominance. The additive-keyed items key to J (Q2), K (Q3) and L (Q6), and the value-keyed items focus M (Q1), J (Q4) and K (Q5) - each additive is the subject of at least one key. That deliberate one-of-each spread is itself the only cross-item pattern I can name: with three letter-keyed items and four letters, a student who has answered two of them can narrow the third to the two unused letters. That is a genuine but weak tell, inherent to a 6-item single-passage set with four labelled series, and I would not hold the batch for it - it would disappear in a full 7-passage form. The stronger issue is the Q1/Q5 value reuse recorded under Q5.
